claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has low hardness and strength because Ti reduces its stacking-fault energy.
Reduced stacking-fault energy produces wider partial-dislocation separation and stacking-fault ribbons.
The Ti-induced dislocation configuration enhances cross-slip and climb.
Enhanced cross-slip and climb accelerate dynamic recovery under load.
Dynamic recovery limits dislocation-density accumulation and work hardening.
Limited dislocation accumulation and work hardening yield lower hardness and strength.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is equimolar, as-cast and homogenized.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is a single-phase FCC solid solution with no observed second phases.
The starting alloy has a grain size of approximately 50–150 µm.
Identically processed equimolar CoCrFeNi is an appropriate Ti-free control for isolating the effect of Ti.
Relative to CoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiTi will have approximately 15–25% lower nanoindentation hardness.
Relative to CoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiTi will have approximately twice as wide stacking faults under TEM.
After identical deformation, CoCrFeNiTi will have approximately 30–50% lower dislocation density than CoCrFeNi.
CoCrFeNi is expected to show higher hardness and narrower stacking faults than CoCrFeNiTi under the same conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature to single-phase FCC microstructures with grain sizes of 50–150 µm, indentation depths below 5 µm, and microcompression strains below 10%.
The magnitude of the Ti-induced stacking-fault-energy reduction has not been directly measured.
Microsegregation or short-range ordering may alternatively affect dislocation behavior in CoCrFeNiTi.

Failure to observe broader stacking faults, or observation of equal or higher post-deformation dislocation density in CoCrFeNiTi despite lower hardness, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
